name: camel-role-play
context: Multi-agent collaboration where agents adopt distinct social roles (e.g., a software architect and a frontend developer) and communicate autonomously to solve a task. Agents are given their role descriptions and the task goal, and they negotiate, delegate, and synthesize results through natural language dialogue. A human operator sets the initial roles and goal but takes no part in the deliberation. Unlike supervisor-worker (hierarchical delegation) or debate (adversarial), role-play agents engage in cooperative dyadic dialogue.
benefits: Exploits role specialization for higher-quality outputs
Agents self-coordinate without a central orchestrator
Dialogue structure mirrors real-world team collaboration
Flexible — roles can be any domain expertise combination
tradeoffs: Unbounded dialogue can drift from the task goal
Harder to predict and audit than structured pipelines
Requires careful role specification to avoid conflicting instructions
Dialogue length grows quickly, increasing latency and cost
use_cases: AI writing team with specialized writer and editor agents
Code review with separate architect and reviewer roles
Research synthesis with scientist and synthesizer agents
Product design with separate UX and engineering agents
avoid_when: Tasks are too simple to benefit from role specialization
Regulated domains requiring auditable structured outputs
anti_patterns: Under-specified roles leading to role confusion
No final answer extraction from dialogue
design_principles: Specify roles with clear responsibilities and constraints
Limit total dialogue turns to prevent infinite loops
Designate one agent to produce the final synthesis
best_practices: Start with a minimal task to calibrate role descriptions
Set a maximum number of dialogue rounds with a fallback synthesizer
Log the full dialogue for post-hoc analysis and debugging
references: Li et al., CAMEL: Communicative Agents for 'Mind' Exploration of Large Language Model Society, NeurIPS 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17760
